title: Veterinary Abbreviations List: The Ones You See in Records Every Day
summary: A practical list of veterinary abbreviations for exams, history, plans, and dosing, in the order they appear in a record, plus the pairs that cause mix-ups.
body_markdown:
Veterinary abbreviations are shortened medical terms and phrases used in medical records to write down findings, procedures, and dosing instructions. They help veterinary teams save time when documenting an exam. However, no official list of veterinary abbreviations exists, and some abbreviations vary from one practice to the next.


For example:


exam


BAR, MM pink, CRT <2 sec, BCS 5/9, T 102.5, HR 125, RR 25


_


This simply means the patient is bright, alert, and responsive (BAR). Mucous membranes (MM) are pink, and capillary refill time (CRT) is less than 2 seconds. The body condition score (BCS) is 5 out of 9. Temperature (T) is in degrees Fahrenheit, heart rate (HR) in beats per minute, and respiratory rate (RR) in breaths per minute.


Other common veterinary abbreviations include WNL (within normal limits), Hx (history), DDx (Differential Diagnosis), Tx (treatment), and Rx (prescription).


These abbreviations exist for a practical reason: the same phrases recur for every patient, and records are often written between appointments rather than after.


## Exam and vitals abbreviations


The following abbreviations are common in the physical exam section of small-animal medical records, though specific wording may vary by practice.


Abbreviation Meaning How it appears in a record


BAR Bright, Alert, Responsive BAR, MM pink and moist, well-hydrated, CRT under 2 seconds.


QAR Quiet, Alert, Responsive QAR on presentation, tolerated exam without resistance, ambulatory on all four limbs.


WNL Within Normal Limits Thoracic auscultation WNL; no murmur or crackles.


NSF No Significant Findings Abdomen soft and non-painful; NSF on palpation.


MM Mucous Membranes MM pink and moist.


CRT Capillary Refill Time CRT <2 seconds.


BCS Body Condition Score BCS 6/9, mildly overweight; weight plan discussed with the owner.


MCS Muscle Condition Score MCS mild loss over the temporal and epaxial muscles.


T/P/R Temperature/Pulse/Respiration T/P/R 101.5F / 120 bpm / 24 brpm.


EENT Eyes, Ears, Nose, Throat EENT WNL, no ocular or aural discharge.


These abbreviations are not universal. Some practices use slightly different abbreviations and combinations of terms. For example, BAR and QAR describe mental status, and some practices add an "H" for hydrated (BARH). In many clinics, WNL and NSF are used interchangeably, while others prefer NAD (no abnormality detected). ADR ("ain't doing right") is sometimes used to describe general malaise.


BCS depends on the scale. Most clinics use the 9-point scale, but some use the 5-point scale. BCS is written as a fraction (for example, 6/9), while MCS is usually recorded as normal, mild, moderate, or severe loss.


The traditional T/P/R is gradually being replaced in modern veterinary records by recording temperature (T), heart rate (HR), and respiratory rate (RR) as separate entries. This removes any doubt about whether "P" means pulse or heart rate, which can differ. In US clinical settings, units are usually left out, and temperature is assumed to be in Fahrenheit.


## Medical history and plan abbreviations


After the physical exam, you'll find several abbreviations throughout the patient's history, assessment, and plan. Learn these in context, because several look similar but mean different things.


Abbreviation Meaning How it appears in a record


Hx History Hx of vomiting for 2 days, no diarrhea, eating normally.


PE Physical Exam PE performed, findings below. Or: PE: BAR, MM pink and moist, heart and lungs NSF.


Dx Diagnosis Dx: acute gastroenteritis.


DDx Differential Diagnoses DDx: dietary indiscretion, foreign body, pancreatitis.


R/O Rule Out R/O foreign body with abdominal radiographs.


Tx Treatment Tx discussed with the owner; started supportive care and antiemetic therapy.


Rx Prescription Rx: amoxicillin PO BID for 7 days.


Sx Signs/Symptoms or Surgery Sx include vomiting and lethargy. (Symptoms) / Sx planned for next week. (Surgery)


POC Plan of Care POC: bloodwork today, recheck in 48 hours.


### Commonly confused pairs


**Dx vs DDx:** Dx is the final diagnosis, while DDx lists the possible causes or conditions being considered before reaching a final diagnosis.


**Tx vs Rx:** Tx refers to treatment given to the patient in the clinic, such as fluids, injections, and wound care. Rx means the prescribed therapy or medication, usually sent home with the pet owner. Some clinics use Rx for both, so always check your clinic's habits.


**Sx:** Pay close attention to Sx. Context usually makes the meaning clear, but on its own, Sx can be ambiguous. In some clinics it means surgery; in others, signs or symptoms.


**POC:** In veterinary medicine, POC generally means "point of care" or "plan of care." In a laboratory context, it can also mean "point of care," as in point-of-care testing.


## Dosing and route abbreviations


This group of abbreviations requires the most caution. A single misreading can lead to a serious medication error, such as a missed dose, a double dose, or the wrong route of administration, any of which can harm a patient.


Abbreviation Meaning How it appears in a record


SID Once daily Rx: antibiotic PO SID for 7 days.


BID Twice daily Ear medication AU BID as directed.


TID Three times daily Rx: analgesic PO TID with food.


QID Four times daily Eye ointment OS QID until recheck.


q12h Every 12 hours Antibiotic PO q12h, doses spaced evenly.


EOD Every other day Medication PO EOD, alternating days.


PRN As needed Anti-nausea tablet PO PRN vomiting.


PO By mouth/orally Medication given PO with breakfast.


SQ/SC Subcutaneous Fluids given SQ over the shoulders.


IM Intramuscular Injection given IM in the epaxial muscles.


IV Intravenous Medication given IV via cephalic catheter.


OU / OS / OD Both eyes / left eye / right eye Drops OU, or OS only if one eye is affected.


### Abbreviations that are easy to misread


The frequency abbreviations SID, BID, TID, QID, EOD, q12h, and PRN need extra care. When handwritten, SID can look like BID. Similarly, the eye abbreviations OU, OS, and OD look alike at a glance and are easy to swap.


## Abbreviations clients shouldn't see: writing them out in discharges


The veterinary record is written in shorthand. The discharge sheet, on the other hand, is what the client takes home, so it should be written in plain language anyone can understand.


Here's the same visit written both ways.


In the veterinary record:


record


BAR, MM pink and moist, CRT <2 sec. Dx: gastroenteritis. Tx: supportive care. Rx: meds PO TID. Recheck PRN.


_


On the discharge:


discharge


Your pet was bright, alert and responsive today. The gums are pink and moist, with a normal capillary refill time. The diagnosis is gastroenteritis. Supportive care was provided. Give the prescribed medication by mouth three times daily as directed. Contact the clinic if you have concerns or if your pet's condition changes.


_


Writing a discharge means decoding the veterinary record into medication instructions, post-operative care, monitoring, vaccine reaction guidance, and follow-up, which takes time. It's the same routine, patient after patient. Retyping "twice a day, morning and evening" or "contact the clinic if you have concerns" takes only a few seconds each time, but it adds up to minutes that clinical staff could spend on patient care.
